options: Running the same query twice and getting a different set of rows back
Reading another transaction's uncommitted, never-committed change
Reading the same row twice within one transaction and getting two different committed values, because another transaction committed an update in between
A query that fails to execute a second time
questions.explain: A nonrepeatable read is about the same row's value changing between two reads in one transaction, due to another transaction's committed update landing in between.

questions.q: How is a nonrepeatable read different from a dirty read?
options: The value read the second time is real and fully committed, unlike a dirty read's never-committed value
A nonrepeatable read involves reading a different row, not the same row
A nonrepeatable read can only happen under SERIALIZABLE
There is no difference -- they are the same anomaly
questions.explain: Unlike a dirty read, the second value Session A sees in a nonrepeatable read is legitimate, committed data -- the problem is that it changed mid-transaction.

questions.q: In the timeline, why does READ COMMITTED still allow Session A's second read to return a different value?
options: READ COMMITTED releases its shared locks as soon as each statement's read finishes, not held for the whole transaction
READ COMMITTED allows dirty reads, which caused the mismatch
Session B's UPDATE was never actually committed
READ COMMITTED does not support SELECT statements inside a transaction
questions.explain: Under READ COMMITTED, the lock from Session A's first read is released right after that statement completes, leaving room for Session B's UPDATE to commit before Session A's second read.

questions.q: Which isolation level is the first to prevent nonrepeatable reads?
options: READ UNCOMMITTED
None of the standard levels prevent it
REPEATABLE READ
READ COMMITTED
questions.explain: REPEATABLE READ holds shared locks on rows it has read until the transaction ends, blocking any other transaction's update to those rows until it finishes.

questions.q: Which isolation levels allow a nonrepeatable read to occur?
options: READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED
All isolation levels allow it
Only READ UNCOMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE
questions.explain: READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED (SQL Server's default) both release or never take the locks needed to prevent another transaction's committed update from slipping in between two reads.
